card.hook: At El Chorro the whole town tips downhill below you, so one photo can hold old stone, an open plaza and a sea of rooftops. You'll earn the view with a few stairs, but it's worth it.
card.stand_here: Go to the exterior atrium of the Capilla de la Santa Cruz del Chorro, right at the phone icon on the map. Face out over the plaza so the chapel is beside you and the town falls away below.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the chapel and its plaza together. Tap 0.5x to squeeze in more plaza and the town below, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for close-ups of the old stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the chapel on one third of the frame, and let the plaza and town fill the rest.
card.best_time: Go early in the day, as one guide suggests. It's a steep climb, so give yourself time and wear comfy shoes.
card.selfie_here: Try the atrium of the chapel, which guides call a prime photo spot with panoramic city views, or the small square in front of the Lavaderos del Chorro chapel, which one guide calls perfect for photoshoots. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and check the landmark is over your shoulder before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: The chapel is a place of worship, so dress respectfully and check access first, as it can be limited during private events. Photo rules inside vary, so look for signs or ask permission, especially during services.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the plaza first, then walk closer and find a single stone detail on the chapel that nobody else would photograph.
card.good_to_know: The chapel dates from the 16th century and has a small plaza in front of it. The atrium is a quieter spot for photos than the lookout further up the hill. Nearby, the Lavaderos del Chorro are red colonial washing basins with a tower and fountains, and Parque El Chorro has winding red walls and a switchback street.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the exterior atrium of the Capilla de la Santa Cruz del Chorro, right at the phone icon on the map. Face out over the plaza so the chapel is beside you and the town falls away below.

card.hook: Picture a church that looks like it was dipped in strawberry milk. That's the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel, and it sits right in the middle of town, so you really can't miss it.
card.stand_here: Head for Jardín Allende and stand on the north-west side of the plaza, across the square from the church. Face south and the whole pink front and both towers fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural look. If the towers get chopped off, tap 0.5x to fit everything in, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the spires and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines, keeping your phone upright so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Go at golden hour or early morning, when the pink stone glows and the square is quieter. It's lit at night too, so an evening shot from the square is worth a try (use night mode and rest your phone on a bench or wall).
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera in Jardín Allende, on the garden side and slightly off to one side of the busiest walkway, so the church stays behind your shoulder without a crowd. For fewer people, try the quieter stretch of Calle Aldama slightly uphill, where the towers still peek into the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the garden side of Jardín Allende, across the street from the church front, while you stand with the church behind you so the whole façade and both towers fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: On Calle Aldama, stay at the edge of the pavement rather than in the middle of the cobbled road. Plaza events can change how busy it is, so allow a little extra time.
card.challenge: Get both towers dead straight against the gridlines, then try to keep one friendly stranger out of the shot. Bonus points for a perfect empty-looking square.
card.good_to_know: The church has a neo-Gothic façade with pointed towers, all in pink stone. For a different view, Calle Aldama looks down a street of colourful colonial façades to the spires, and El Mirador, higher up, shows the church rising above the rooftops. The façade can be photographed from the open square, but check locally if you want to go inside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Jardín Allende and stand on the north-west side of the plaza, across the square from the church. Face south and the whole pink front and both towers fit in one frame.

selfie_spots.why: A proposal guide says this spot keeps the pink church in the frame without the crowd, which also suits a selfie with the facade behind you.

card.hook: Six old mansions have been stitched together into one hotel here, so you're not photographing a single building, you're photographing a whole stretch of stone, colour and cobbles. It's one of those streets where almost any angle looks good.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Cuna de Allende, about 220 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Shoot from the street, looking towards the buildings.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the street and buildings as you find them. Drop to 0.5x only if the street is narrow and you need the full height of a facade, and hold your phone level so the walls don't lean. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for carved doorways, windows and rooftop details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep walls and doorways straight, then tap the brightest sunlit wall and slide the brightness down a touch so the stone keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the stone and paintwork look warmer. Midday sun makes deep shadows in narrow streets.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the street, and keep the old stone frontage behind your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher than your eyes and keep the walls straight against the gridlines.
card.rules_and_safety: The hotel is private property and the courtyards may be limited to guests, so check the official site before you go if you hope to see inside. The streets around it are public, so keep your shots to what you can see from there, and be polite about any guests or staff who wander into the frame.
card.challenge: Take one wide street shot, then hunt down three details close up: a doorway, a stone arch and a patch of wall colour you'd happily paint your own house.
card.good_to_know: Belmond Casa de Sierra Nevada is made up of six colonial mansions in the middle of San Miguel de Allende. They include a 17th-century fort, the 18th-century Casa Palma and a house said to have been the archbishop's residence in the 16th century. The wider town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which is why so many streets around here look good in a frame.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle Cuna de Allende, about 220 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Shoot from the street, looking towards the buildings.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the hotel behind the visitor, so I have not listed one. The hotel pages are mostly marketing galleries and reviews. The Hisugarplum blog (https://hisugarplum.com/casa-de-sierra-nevada/) describes a photo shoot in and around the property without naming a specific spot. No page I found gives selfie-stick or tripod rules, and none gives a safety point for this spot. Searches were limited, so a travel blog or photo guide that names a specific corner or street may still exist.

card.hook: The carved saints on this church seem to be watching the plaza, and you'll want to show them off. The Baroque front of Templo de San Francisco is the star, so give it room.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de San Francisco, in front of the main façade, and look north. Step back until the whole church fits, with a strip of open plaza at the bottom of your photo.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the whole façade fits. Use 0.5x only if you're very close, and keep the church in the middle so the edges don't stretch it. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved saints and the fancy stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the church and doorway with the vertical lines so the façade doesn't lean, leaving a little room above the top.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is likely to give softer light on the stonework and a calmer plaza. Check how the light hits the façade when you arrive, because it changes through the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the sunken courtyard in front of the façade, near the benches and the shaded edge of the plaza. Use the front camera (0.5x if you want more church in the shot) and let the carved front rise up over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the plaza in front of the façade, far enough back to fit the full front and its tower, while you pose in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, and photography rules apply inside, so ask before you take pictures in the interior. One general guide to San Miguel churches says photos without flash are usually fine outside services, but flash may be restricted. Opening hours vary, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom to 5x (if your phone has it) and find your favourite carved saint, then take one photo of just them.
card.good_to_know: The Templo de San Francisco stands at the corner of San Francisco and Juárez streets, facing Plaza de San Francisco. Its Baroque façade is known for carved saints and Churrigueresque detail. For a second picture, walk to that corner for a closer, angled view of the side and front, where the stonework shows more depth and texture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de San Francisco, in front of the main façade, and look north. Step back until the whole church fits, with a strip of open plaza at the bottom of your photo.

card.hook: You wander through a plaza with a café and a few galleries, wind your way through old courtyards, and then the spires of the Parroquia pop up over the roofline like they were waiting for you. That's the moment to stop and get your phone out.
card.stand_here: Head for the Instituto Allende, a few blocks southwest of the town centre, and walk through the front plaza to the back courtyard. Stand at the phone icon on the map and face the church spires showing above the building.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole courtyard view toward the Parroquia, then try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to bring the spires closer. Switch to 0.5x among the arches, fountain and murals, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the Parroquia, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the spires don't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light in the courtyard. Honestly, though, whether the courtyard is open matters more than the hour.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the courtyard in front of the Ignacio Allende mural, so the school's art fills the background. Or stand beside the courtyard fountain with the colonial building rising behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little higher than your face.
card.rules_and_safety: Courtyards or the terrace can close for weddings or private events, so check when you arrive. The private chapel sits behind locked grates and isn't a viewpoint. This is a working art school, so keep a gentle pace and leave students and classes undisturbed.
card.challenge: Take a three-shot set: an arch, a splash of bougainvillea, and the fountain, all without a single student in the frame.
card.good_to_know: The Canal family began building this huge house in 1735 as a country residence. In 1809 it passed to the Discalced Carmelite sisters. The art school opened in 1950 and still fills the rear of the complex and its gardens.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Instituto Allende, a few blocks southwest of the town centre, and walk through the front plaza to the back courtyard. Stand at the phone icon on the map and face the church spires showing above the building.

card.hook: Calle Mesones is narrow, old and busy, and that's exactly why this shot works. The theatre's 1915 facade sits in the middle of a proper colonial street, so one photo gives you the building and the town.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Mesones in the historic centre and face south, because the theatre lies to the south of you along the street. For a straight-on view, cross to the opposite side near the facade and stop opposite its centre.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front into the tight street, then try 1x for a more natural look. Switch to 2x for the doorway and the upper part of the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the building's vertical edges, then keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually quieter on a narrow street, so the facade is easier to get clear. When you arrive, check how the light falls on the front, and if the sky behind looks bright, tap the facade and slide it a touch darker so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the sidewalk in front of the facade at Mesones 82, on the corner with Hernández Macías. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it), hold it a little low and keep the theatre over your shoulder. The street is tight, so check on the ground how much of the building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The street is a public place to stand and photograph. If you want to go inside the theatre, check opening details locally before you go.
card.challenge: Mesones is busy, so be patient: wait for the gap between passers-by and grab a clean, empty street in front of the facade.
card.good_to_know: The theatre's classical facade dates from 1915, and it's the main thing to photograph. It sits on Calle Mesones in the historic centre of San Miguel de Allende. The narrow colonial street and its old buildings make a natural frame around it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle Mesones in the historic centre and face south, because the theatre lies to the south of you along the street. For a straight-on view, cross to the opposite side near the facade and stop opposite its centre.

card.hook: Pink stone usually looks a bit washed out on a phone screen, but not here. This church glows, and the towers and dome make a lively outline against the sky.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza Cívica, the small open square next to the church, and face the pink facade. Walk a little until the towers sit clear above the roofline, and take a few steps back so the tops don't get cut off.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the facade and towers together. If the square feels too tight, tap 0.5x, and try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the carving and tower details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up a tower or the edge of the facade with a vertical line, so the building doesn't look like it's leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the pink stone and fewer people in the square. Check how the light falls on the day.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the small square right in front of the pink main facade, with the facade and towers behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and hold the phone a bit higher so the towers fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Calle Insurgentes, a little back from the facade, so the whole church, towers and dome included, fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside is subject to local rules and flash is discouraged, so check the rules before you take your phone out indoors. It's a place of worship, so dress modestly, and if a Mass is under way, keep your distance from anyone entering or leaving.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the tallest tower sits dead straight on a gridline with a little sky above it. Bonus points if nobody's head is in the way.
card.good_to_know: The Oratorio de San Felipe Neri is a church in San Miguel de Allende, known for its pink baroque facade, several towers and its dome. Calle Insurgentes shows it rising above the street with the town's skyline behind it. The outside is your main photo, so treat the inside as a bonus.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza Cívica, the small open square next to the church, and face the pink facade. Walk a little until the towers sit clear above the roofline, and take a few steps back so the tops don't get cut off.

card.hook: You climb up, you turn around, and there it is: one pink church sitting in a sea of rooftops with hills behind it. It's the classic San Miguel de Allende view, and it's easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the main lookout platform at Salida Real a Querétaro 92. Face out over the historic centre so the pink Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel is your main landmark.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole town and the hills in. Then try 1x for a natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Parroquia and the rooftops around it.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the town, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky keeps its colour at sunset.
card.best_time: Sunset or golden hour is the favourite, and the town lights come on after that. The platform gets crowded around sunset, so arrive a little early to claim a spot. One guide also suggests early morning.
card.selfie_here: Head to the safety fence on the main lookout, where the love locks hang. It's a popular photo stop. Use your front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and turn so the town is over your shoulder. It's busy with selfie-takers, so be patient.
card.rules_and_safety: Check locally for any closures or restrictions before you go. If you walk up, check the route on your map first.
card.challenge: Put the Parroquia on a gridline crossing, keep the horizon level, then sneak in a little branch at the edge as a natural frame.
card.good_to_know: El Mirador is a free public lookout, and guides call it the classic panoramic spot in town. If a branch blocks your view, take a step or two along the platform. For a prettier walk up, Callejón del Chorro has colourful terraced houses, plants and narrow alleys.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, on the main lookout platform at Salida Real a Querétaro 92. Face out over the historic centre so the pink Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel is your main landmark.

selfie_research.notes: Selfie spots are the two places the pages name, but neither gives a precise standing point with the mirador behind the visitor, so treat them as areas on the lookout. No page I found names a spot for a passer-by to photograph a visitor with the whole mirador in frame, so ask_someone_spot is null. Pages also disagree on the address (Salida Real a Querétaro 92 on several listings, 90 on one). No page states rules on selfie sticks or tripods; one guide only says a tripod can help for low-light shots, which is advice, not a rule. Several pages say the lookout is crowded with selfie-takers and that the walk is steep, but none gives a safety instruction.

card.hook: Look up. Among all the buildings around the square, there's a statue standing on a second-floor perch, and that's your sign you've found Ignacio Allende's old house.
card.stand_here: Stand in the southwest corner of Jardín Allende, about 54 m from Casa de Allende. Face south-west and you'll see the facade with the statue, framed by the corner of the square.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole facade and the statue together. Then try 2x or more (depends on your phone) to bring the statue closer without crossing the square. Save 0.5x for when you want lots of square in the shot, and keep the house away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the statue near an upper third line, and keep the phone level so the building edges stay straight.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the facade is evenly lit and the square is quieter. If glare or shadow lands on the statue, shuffle a few steps along the corner and check again.
card.selfie_here: Head to the street corner where the Casa de Allende building meets the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel, a corner a photo blog calls popular for photographs. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if you want more in the frame, and keep the museum building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone in Jardín Allende, the main square across from the parish church, to take your photo, then check the house made it into the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open to everyone, but the museum inside the house may have its own photo rules, so check with the museum before shooting indoors.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close shot of the statue, then see which one you'd actually put on the fridge.
card.good_to_know: Casa de Allende is the house where Ignacio Allende lived, and today it's a museum at Cuna de Allende 1. For a different angle, climb the steps of the Iglesia de San Rafael: the house sits behind you and La Parroquia appears at the left of the frame.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the southwest corner of Jardín Allende, about 54 m from Casa de Allende. Face south-west and you'll see the facade with the statue, framed by the corner of the square.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is supported by a page; no page says exactly where a selfie-taker should stand with the museum behind them, so the corner is the best available match. The ask-someone spot (Jardín Allende) is named by pages for photographing the parish church across the street; no page confirms it frames the whole Casa de Allende, so treat it as unverified for that. No page states any selfie stick or tripod rule. One Wanderlog reviewer reports a fee to take photos inside the museum (65 pesos in one review, 60 in another) and a 70 MXN entrance in a third, so these figures conflict and should be checked on site. The museum is listed at Cuna de Allende 1, Zona Centro, which pages place on the corner with the main church. I could not confirm that the supplied coordinates (20.91387, -100.74417) match that address.
